title: What is known about 1RB0RE_1RC---_0RD0RC_1LE1LF_1LD1RA_1RC0LF
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RE_1RC---_0RD0RC_1LE1LF_1LD1RA_1RC0LF.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The run is a sequence of phases; in each, rounds (proved in Lean) move two 10s from a stack into a growing gap of 0s, and at the end the gap is turned back into a stack about 3/2 times as large. The phase map, checked by simulation for every x ≤ 120 in the decoded cases, takes the blank-tape orbit through 63 phases, to P(1, 2,162,240,868,156,300); the next phase is in the case x ≡ 4 (mod 8) with the leading 1, which splits further by higher powers of 2 (e.g. 32i + 20 → 243i + 202) and was not decoded.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (B1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: Rounds of a phase
claims.text: With the stack (10)x+2 1 1 1 0, a gap of 2g + 2 zeros and D at the right end, one round removes two 10s and adds six zeros: (10)x+2 1110 (00)g 00 D> → (10)x 1110 (00)g+3 00 D> in 4g + 26 steps (and the first round, from no gap, in 22 steps). Plus the shift rules: C erases 1s going right, D and E fill 0s going left.

claims.title: The phase map
claims.text: P(pre, x) = [1] (10)x 1110 D> at the right end of blank tape. Checked by direct simulation for all 225 decoded cases with x ≤ 120: P(0, x) → P(x mod 2, 3⌊x/2⌋ + 6); P(1, 2i+1) → P(0, 3i + 6); P(1, 4i+2) → P(1, 9i + 15); P(1, 8i) → P(1, 27i + 18). The slopes 3/2, 9/4, 27/8 are powers of 3/2.

claims.title: 63 phases, then the undecoded case
claims.text: From blank tape the machine reaches P(1, 3) at step 34; the map then gives P(0, 9), P(1, 18), P(1, 51), P(0, 81), P(1, 126), P(1, 294), P(1, 672), P(1, 2286), P(1, 5154), P(1, 11607), P(0, 17415), ... (the first 14 agree with the run to 1.8·10<sup>9</sup> steps) and stays in the decoded cases for 63 phases, to P(1, 2,162,240,868,156,300), which is ≡ 4 (mod 8). The map itself is only checked for small x, so the long orbit is a prediction, not a proof.

claims.title: The case P(1, 8i+4)
claims.text: It splits further: 32i + 20 → P(0, 243i + 202) and 32i + 28 → P(0, 243i + 264) for i ≤ 3 (243 = 3<sup>5</sup>, 32 = 2<sup>5</sup>), while 4 → P(0, 193), 12 → P(1, 3771), 36 → P(1, 492), and 44, 68 take more than 10<sup>8</sup> steps. No halt in any of these runs.

claims.title: Where it can halt
claims.text: Only B reading 1 halts; B is entered only from A reading 0, and A only from E reading 1, so the machine halts exactly on E> 1 0 1. Read off the table.

claims.title: No closed tape language with small windows
claims.text: bbtools.ctl K = 3..6 leaves halting configurations; n-gram CPS 3 to 7 fails; no invariant mod 2..12.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 63,228 cells have been visited and 26,115 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.051). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.496).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The decoded cases multiply x by (3/2)k; which case applies depends on the low binary digits of x, and each further level of 2-adic digits brings another factor 3/2. Deciding halting means understanding this map on all of its 2-adic levels (and whether some level produces E> 1 0 1), a Collatz-type problem.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has run for 10<sup>9</sup> steps without stopping. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and lists what is known, each result marked by what it rests on.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 63,228 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: A stack of 10s and a gap of 0s
html:
At the start of a phase the tape is [1] (10)x 1 1 1 0 with the head in state D just right of it; call it P(pre, x), pre = 1 when the leading 1 is there. The blank-tape run is at P(1, 3) after 34 steps, P(0, 9) after 139, P(1, 18) after 520, P(1, 51) after 3,606.

During a phase, at step 108 for instance: 

1 0 0 (10)^3408 1 1 1 0 0^2590 [D0] 1^10388
a stack of 10s, a gap of 0s that grows, and (in some phases) a run of 1s further right.

sections.heading: Two 10s out, six 0s in; then the gap becomes the new stack
html: Each round the head goes from the right end to the top of the stack and back: two copies of 10 leave the stack and the gap grows by six 0s (proved in Lean, 4g + 26 steps). When the stack is empty, the gap of about 3x zeros is turned into a stack of about 3x/2 copies of 10. So in the simplest case P(0, x) → P(x mod 2, 3⌊x/2⌋ + 6).

With the leading 1 present and x even, the end of the phase goes through more levels: P(1, 4i+2) → P(1, 9i + 15), P(1, 8i) → P(1, 27i + 18), and x = 8i + 4 splits again by 32 (slope 243/32). The slopes are 3/2, 9/4, 27/8, ..., 243/32: each extra power of 2 dividing x adds a factor 3/2.

Worked example: P(1, 18), 18 = 4·4 + 2, goes to P(1, 9·4 + 15) = P(1, 51); 51 is odd, so P(0, 3·25 + 6) = P(0, 81); 81 with pre = 0 gives P(1, 3·40 + 6) = P(1, 126). These are exactly the phase starts of the real run.

sections.heading: 63 phases in the decoded cases
html: Iterating the map from P(1, 3), the orbit stays in the decoded cases for 63 phases and reaches P(1, 2,162,240,868,156,300), which is 4 mod 8, the first case without a formula. The map was checked against the machine for every decoded case with x ≤ 120, not proved, so this is a strong prediction rather than a theorem.
The machine can only stop on E> 1 0 1. Whether it does is a question about this (3/2)k map on all levels of the binary digits of x: of the same kind as the Collatz problem.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.051). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.496).
After 109 steps the tape spans 63,228 cells (24 left of the start, 45,538 right), with a density of 1s of 0.413.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: A Collatz-like map that multiplies by powers of 3/2: phase starts [1] (10)^x 1110 go to x' ≈ (3/2)^k·x, with k set by the low binary digits of x; the orbit from blank tape stays in the decoded cases for 63 phases, up to x ≈ 2.2·10^15.
